content: MarkTechPost https://www.marktechpost.com/ An Artificial Intelligence News Platform Wed, 11 Nov 2026 15:51:16 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.marktechpost.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/cropped-Favicon-512-x-512-1-1-32x32.png MarkTechPost https://www.marktechpost.com/ 32 32 127842392 Marktechpost AI Launches GPU Leaderboard and the Deploy It Chrome Extension https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/11/11/marktechpost-gpu-leaderboard-chrome-extension-launch/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 15:51:14 +0000 https://www.marktechpost.com/?p=83854 Marktechpost Launches GPU Leaderboard and the Deploy It Chrome Extension The post Marktechpost AI Launches GPU Leaderboard and the Deploy It Chrome Extension appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Marktechpost has launched GPU Leaderboard , a free cloud GPU price comparison for AI inference. It also shipped GPU Leaderboard: Deploy It , a Chrome extension for the same data. The site reads on-demand and spot prices from each provider’s own pricing page. The goal is simple: answer “what GPU do I need, and where is it cheapest?” in one place. What is GPU Leaderboard? GPU Leaderboard is a pricing dashboard that ranks rentable cloud GPUs by price per GPU-hour. It is built for teams running inference. The v1 application has 4 views: Inference pricing: a cost calculator for a full run, not a single hourly rate. Leaderboard : every offer ranked by $/GPU-hr, filterable by GPU, tier, region and availability. Cheapest Inference : the lowest on-demand floor for each tracked GPU. Providers : a directory with instance counts, regions, status-page incidents and price-check history. How does the GPU inference cost calculator work? You pick an accelerator, GPU count, duration and utilization. The calculator then prices that exact run at every provider. An optional model field narrows the list. The default example is 8×H100 for 72 hours at 90% utilization. That bills 576 GPU-hours. The cheapest result is $967.68 at Latitude, at $1.68 per GPU-hour. The median across 15 providers is $1,716.48. The most expensive is $3,545.28 at CoreWeave. The calculator also shows a “real” cost per used GPU-hour. Idle time is still billed, so $1.68 at 90% utilization becomes $1.87. This is the number most budget sheets miss. What does the Deploy It Chrome extension do? GPU Leaderboard: Deploy It brings the price data to where developers pick models. Per its store listing, it works in 3 places: Hugging Face model pages: detects model size and estimates VRAM at FP16, INT8 and INT4. It then shows the cheapest hourly GPUs that fit. GitHub repos: detects model references and gives a hardware estimate in place. Toolbar lookup: search any model or GPU from the browser toolbar. Key Takeaways GPU Leaderboard ranks 201 live GPU offers from 24 providers by $/GPU-hr. Its calculator prices a full run, including idle time at your utilization. Deploy It shows VRAM needs and cheapest GPUs on Hugging Face and GitHub. An 8×H100, 72-hour run spans $967.68 to $3,545.28 across multiple providers. Coverage and daily refresh are the main gaps versus older trackers. Try it at gpuleaderboard.com and install the Deploy It extension from the Chrome Web Store. The post MBZUAI’s IFM Releases PAN 2, an Open 29B World Model for Physical AI appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> The Institute of Foundation Models (IFM) at MBZUAI released PAN 2 , an open world model for physical intelligence. The PAN 2 world model takes a scene and a text action and simulates the outcome as video. IFM announced it on X on November 10, 2026. Weights, training code and inference code ship under Apache 2.0 . For robotics and agent developers, the pitch is simple: test a plan in simulation before acting on it. TL;DR Size: 29B-parameter diffusion transformer (MMDiT), dense. Inputs: text plus an optional first frame. Output: 704×1248 video at 24 fps, up to 20 s. Runs on: Data-center GPUs. Each worker holds the full 29B model in BF16, with block offloading as fallback. Performance: Leads 6 tested models on full plans. Trails MiniMax-H3 on single actions and human preference. Best: 34.0% full-plan completion on 100 multi-step tasks, the highest of all models tested (self-reported). Worst: About 2 in 3 plans miss a step. Physics-IQ system default: 37.48 vs 42.91 for MiniMax-H3. Bottom line: Best: a fully open world model that leads on multi-step plans. Worst: long plans still fail often, and hardware needs are high. What is PAN 2? PAN 2 is a general-purpose world model from IFM that simulates how a scene changes after an action. It follows the Generative Latent Prediction (GLP) architecture from IFM’s Critique of World Models paper. It succeeds PAN , released in November 2025. The goal is simulative reasoning . An agent proposes plans, PAN 2 simulates each one, and the agent acts on the best. How does PAN 2 work? PAN 2 splits simulation into 2 kinds of reasoning : Conceptual reasoning : An LLM reads the observation and the requested actions. It writes the next world state as structured JSON: events, timed actions bound to actors, and camera motion. Any instruction-following LLM can fill this role. IFM’s report uses Kimi K3 by default. Perceptual reasoning : A 29B MMDiT predicts the video latents. IFM trained it from scratch on hundreds of millions of annotated videos. A frozen Qwen3.5-9B text encoder conditions it. The Wan 2.2 VAE decoder renders the final frames. IFM’s ablation shows the LLM matters. With no conceptual reasoning, full-plan completion drops from 34.0% to 0.0%. Step completion falls from 75.1% to 8.7%. A format-only rewrite recovers part of the gap, reaching 27.8% full-plan completion. IFM also dropped gameplay, animation and simulation footage after early training. A 9B test model trained without it won 58% of blinded votes.
